At about the same time as The Telegraph was in Majdal Zoun on Friday, a four-man IDF tank crew was killed by a suspected Hezbollah drone or rocket attack in Kfar Tebnit, 22 miles to the north-east.

Israel responded with 150 air strikes that it said had killed “dozens of terrorists” across Lebanon.

Kfar Tebnit, like Majdal Zoun, also conceals a large Hezbollah tunnel network, according to Israel media.

The flare-up was seized upon by Israel’s ruling coalition government which faces an election in October and is under significant pressure over the failure of the Iran war.

In Bürgenstock, Switzerland, US and Iranian negotiators, including Mr Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as well as Mr Vance, began 60 days of negotiations.

“The question before us now is how much more can we accomplish together? Can we turn over a new leaf?” Mr Vance asked.

“Can we change relations in the Middle East permanently, or do we go back to doing things the old way, which is not our preference, but is certainly very much something that can happen,” he added.

But just as the negotiations threaten Israel’s freedom of action, they have also sapped the credibility of the Lebanese government, experts say.

Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Centre in Beirut told The Telegraph that the Lebanese government, already weak, was being undermined by both the Israelis and the Iranians, reducing its ability to disarm Hezbollah.

“The Lebanese are paying the price for both sides,” he said. “The Israelis are not that interested in giving them anything that can strengthen the credibility of the Lebanese state, and nor do the Iranians have any interest in giving anything that may make the Lebanese state more credible.”

Although the US’s return to diplomacy has been welcomed by most leaders around the world, primarily because it has reopened the Strait of Hormuz, few believe the issue of the Israel-Lebanon conflict will be resolved any time soon.

The two sides were again trading blows on Saturday. Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, knows he would face electoral oblivion were he to pull the IDF out of Lebanon before the October elections in Israel.

Meanwhile in Lebanon, Iran is tightening its grip on Hezbollah.

“Since the assassination of Hassan Nasrallah back in September 2024, the Iranians have got a tighter control, they’ve been involved with the reorganisation of the Islamic resistance, the military component of Hezbollah, and we’ve seen that visibly over the last three or four months,” said Mr Blanford.

And on both sides people are dying. More than 100 IDF soldiers have been killed in the Israeli-Hezbollah conflict since Oct 7, 2023, and nearly 50 civilians. On the Lebanese side, nearly 4,000 people have lost their lives since March 2 this year alone.
